explanation: Procedure explicitly sets SET NOCOUNT OFF, so every statement sends row-count messages to the client; use SET NOCOUNT ON to reduce network chatter.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF while the procedure opens transactions (lines 182 and 239); a run-time error can leave a transaction partially applied instead of aborting and rolling back.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders couples callers to all 16 columns including nvarchar(MAX) LOBs; explicitly list the required columns to survive schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so which 10 rows are returned is arbitrary and non-repeatable.
DISTINCT on o.OrderID, the primary key of Sales.Orders, forces needless duplicate-elimination work on rows that are already unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders can return uncommitted, missing, or duplicated rows; use READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT instead.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) wraps the indexed OrderDate column in a function, blocking a range seek; rewrite as o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' AND o.OrderDate < '2017-01-01'.
Compares int column Sales.Orders.CustomerID to nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText, forcing an implicit conversion that degrades seeks and cardinality estimates.
(@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID) is a catch-all OR predicate that discourages index seeks and misleads cardinality estimation.
o.Comments LIKE N'%urgent%' begins with a wildcard, forcing a full scan of the nvarchar(MAX) Comments column with no possibility of an index seek.
o.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT i.CustomerID FROM Sales.Invoices) silently returns zero rows if the subquery ever produces a NULL; use NOT EXISTS instead.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps the Sales.Orders.CustomerID column in ISNULL, making the predicate non-sargable and preventing an index seek.
o.OrderID + 0 = @OrderID applies arithmetic to the key column so PK_Sales_Orders cannot be matched directly; compare o.OrderID = @OrderID instead.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is an inequality predicate that typically forces scanning a large portion of Sales.Orders.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and multiplies every order by every customer.
SELECT TOP (1) over the Sales.Orders CROSS JOIN Sales.Customers has no ORDER BY, so the chosen row is arbitrary.

Comma-separated FROM (Sales.Orders AS o, Sales.OrderLines AS ol) with the join condition in WHERE is legacy syntax that obscures intent and invites accidental cartesian joins; use explicit JOIN ... ON.
SELECT TOP (1) from the comma join of Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines has no ORDER BY, making the returned row non-deterministic.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID) runs a scalar lookup per outer Sales.Orders row; a grouped join or window aggregate computes it in one pass.
Correlated EXISTS on Sales.OrderLines (ol.OrderID = o.OrderID AND ol.Quantity > 1) executes per outer row instead of expressing the check as a set join.
CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END is duplicated in the select list and the ORDER BY; order by the alias HasComments so the two copies cannot diverge.
ORDER BY 2 silently points at o.OrderDate; if the Sales.Orders select list changes order, the sort changes without any visible edit. Order by column name.
OFFSET/FETCH orders only by the non-unique o.OrderDate; ties break arbitrarily, so pages can skip or repeat rows. Add a unique tie-breaker such as OrderID.
The two UNION branches filter Sales.Orders on disjoint literals (OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2), so UNION's duplicate-removal sort is wasted work; use UNION ALL.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID) > 0 counts every matching line row when EXISTS would stop at the first match.
The COUNT(*) subquery correlated on ol.OrderID = o.OrderID is a per-row scalar lookup against Sales.OrderLines; express it as a join-based existence check.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders silently keeps an arbitrary (last) row's value when multiple rows are returned; add an exact predicate or TOP (1) with ORDER BY.
@OrderIds table variable has no statistics and is cardinality-estimated as 1 row at older compatibility levels; a #temp table gives the optimizer real distribution information.
SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID filling @OrderIds has no ORDER BY, so which 5 Sales.Orders rows are captured is arbitrary.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders derives the temp-table schema implicitly and can block optimization paths; declare the table explicitly and INSERT into it.
SELECT TOP (5) into #ImplicitOrders has no ORDER BY; the selected Sales.Orders rows are non-deterministic.
order_cursor iterates Sales.Orders rows one at a time; set-based DML over the same keys avoids the cursor's per-row overhead.
The cursor's SELECT TOP (2) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so the fetched rows are arbitrary.
WHILE loop performs iterative per-iteration work instead of a set-based operation.
@Sql is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @CustomerID) into the query text; bind the value as a parameter instead of splicing it into the string.
EXEC (@Sql) runs the concatenated statement with no bound parameters; use sys.sp_executesql with a @CustomerID parameter.
@Sql is assembled by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @OrderID) into the statement text rather than binding the value as a parameter.
sys.sp_executesql is invoked with no parameter list; @OrderID's value was embedded in the string instead of being passed via @params.
#Scratch is created with CREATE TABLE but never dropped, lingering until procedure scope ends; add DROP TABLE #Scratch when finished.
The CATCH block only SELECTs ERROR_MESSAGE() AS IgnoredError; it neither THROWs nor returns a failure status, so the error disappears silently.
RAISERROR(N'Negative order ID', 16, 1) is the legacy error mechanism; use THROW for new error paths to preserve error numbers and rethrow semantics.
PRINT N'Monster procedure diagnostic' is buffered and invisible to most API clients; log to a table or raise a structured error instead.
Business identifier 1 is embedded directly in the predicate o.CustomerID = 1 instead of being accepted as a parameter or looked up.
The bare '20160101' constant in o.OrderDate >= '20160101' encodes an undocumented business date; move it to a well-named parameter or variable.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits the style argument, so the string parses as January 2 or February 1 depending on session language settings; specify style 101/103 or an ISO format.
Join predicate COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) = COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) wraps both keys in COALESCE, preventing index-based join selection between Sales.Orders and Sales.Invoices.
SELECT TOP (1) from the Sales.Orders/Sales.Invoices join has no ORDER BY, so the returned row is arbitrary.
Sales.Orders is joined to itself on o.OrderID = o2.OrderID only to re-fetch the same OrderID already available in o; the join adds cost without new information.
SELECT TOP (1) from the self-join has no ORDER BY, making the chosen Sales.Orders row non-deterministic.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts Sales.Orders by an unselective nvarchar(MAX) column, forcing an expensive sort over wide LOB data.
SELECT SUM(ol.Quantity) scans the entire Sales.OrderLines fact table with no restrictive WHERE predicate; add selective filtering on order, date, or stock item.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 is a row-level predicate on the grouped Sales.OrderLines column; move it to WHERE so rows are filtered before grouping.
COUNT(*) over Sales.Orders without GROUP BY returns exactly one row; the ORDER BY OrderCount adds a needless sort.
MERGE against Sales.Orders has documented concurrency and correctness edge cases (race conditions, failed multi-row matches); use separate UPDATE/INSERT statements.
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET target.Comments = target.Comments writes the identical value back, still generating log records and taking locks on Sales.Orders.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments rewrites the same value, causing needless transaction-log writes and locking with no data change.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 deletes by a non-key business value, risking removal of unintended rows; delete by OrderLineID/OrderID keys.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' parks a worker thread for a second; use asynchronous scheduling rather than sleeping inside T-SQL.
BEGIN TRANSACTION here is not inside a BEGIN TRY/CATCH, so an error before the ROLLBACK can strand an open transaction on the session.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON overrides identity generation and couples the code to manual key management; restrict this to controlled data-load scenarios.
EXEC sp_who invokes the system routine without a schema qualifier, adding name-resolution overhead; call sys.sp_who.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 changes session state and is never restored; the following statement (and anything after) silently returns a single row. Reset with SET ROWCOUNT 0.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories omits an explicit column list; VALUES (99, @NewCategory) breaks silently if the temp table's column order changes.
Category id 99 is hard-coded into the #DemoCategories INSERT instead of being derived from a lookup or passed as a named parameter.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' starts with a wildcard, forcing a scan of Sales.Customers.CustomerName instead of seeking UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
@sql is built by concatenating @CustomerName into the LIKE pattern of the statement text; build the statement statically and bind the pattern as a parameter.
User-supplied @CustomerName is concatenated directly into executable SQL; a value containing a quote escapes the string literal and allows arbitrary SQL injection. Parameterize with sp_executesql.
The LIKE pattern embedded in the dynamic SQL begins with '%', so the resulting query on #DemoCustomers.CustomerName cannot use an index seek.
sp_executesql is called with no @params argument; @CustomerName's value was concatenated into the string rather than bound as a parameter.
EXEC sp_executesql is invoked without a schema qualifier; call sys.sp_executesql to avoid extra name resolution.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 has no WHERE clause and overwrites every row in the table; constrain the update to the intended customers.
CustomerCategoryID is set to the magic value 1 rather than a parameter or a looked-up category key.
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' filters the right side of the LEFT JOIN, silently converting it to an INNER JOIN and dropping Sales.Customers with no orders; move the predicate into the ON clause.
The '2016-01-01' literal is embedded directly in the o.OrderDate predicate with no label or parameter documenting its business meaning.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL never matches any row because equality with NULL yields UNKNOWN; use IS NULL (or a properly handled optional parameter) to get correct results.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) is a scalar UDF evaluated once per Sales.Customers row, forcing row-by-row execution (and serial plans before SQL 2019); inline the logic or use an inline TVF.
The CATCH block only SELECTs ERROR_MESSAGE(); it neither THROWs nor returns a failure status, so the caller never learns the DELETE from #DemoCustomers failed.
The CATCH runs while the transaction begun on line 239 may still be open, yet never issues ROLLBACK; the session can be left with an open, doomed transaction holding locks.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hard-pins Sales.Customers to index id 1, overriding the optimizer; the hint goes stale and harmful as data and indexes change.
CustomerID is selected through three levels of nested derived tables (t1, t2, t3) over Sales.Customers; flatten to a single query or use CTEs for a better plan and readable code.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' starts with a wildcard, so the innermost Sales.Customers access cannot seek UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName and must scan.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) returns every column the function produces; enumerate the required columns to keep the contract stable.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement table-valued function with fixed cardinality guesses and no statistics; rewrite as an inline TVF so the optimizer can inline the logic.
